featured_reviews.review_text:
Trekking Routes & Difficulty

Two main trails:

1. Steeper, direct rocky route—more cardio-intensive, takes 30–40 minutes for average trekkers  .

2. Gradual long-cut path wide enough for two vehicles—gentler, follows a 2-car-wide dusty track  .

Approaching via Sardar Tara Singh Park (aka Tarasingh Garden) or from the Cypress area, morning is ideal to avoid midday guards  .

---

🌿 Trail Ambience & Wildlife

Lush greenery, with monkeys and langurs frequently spotted  .

Natural spring near a hillside temple provides fresh, drinkable water  .

Wildlife warnings include occasional leopard sightings—trekking in groups is safer  .

featured_reviews.review_text:
Today, I got down at Mulund Bus Depot and was pleasantly surprised to find a lush green garden right in front of me. I took a stroll and felt refreshed by the calm atmosphere.
This is Lala Tulsiram Udyan (also known as Lala Tulsi Ram Park), located on Devidayal Road, opposite the BEST Bus Depot in Gavane Pada, Mulund West. It’s about 0.6 km (7–8 minutes on foot) from Mulund railway station. The park is open daily from 6:00 AM to 8:30 PM with free entry through two gates on main roads.
The park features tree-shaded walking paths, regularly pruned hedges, and a clean, peaceful environment—often cleaned three times a day. There’s a foam-padded play area with swings, slides, a jungle gym, and a sandpit for children. For adults, there are benches, clean toilets, drinking water, jogging tracks, and wheelchair access.
It’s a favorite spot for children, joggers, and senior citizens who come to socialize or read newspapers. Locals still cherish it, even though rules have become more relaxed since the BMC took over from a private trust.
Perfect for: a morning walk, children’s play, or a peaceful break in nature.

featured_reviews.review_text: Thane Railway Station is one of the busiest and best-connected stations in the Mumbai region. It offers frequent train services, good facilities, and easy connectivity for daily commuters. The station is generally well-maintained, though it can get very crowded during peak hours.

featured_reviews.name: Govind Sharma
featured_reviews.review_text:
Thane Railway Station is truly one of the most important and busiest stations in the Mumbai suburban network and can rightly be called the lifeline of the city. Located at the heart of Thane, it offers excellent connectivity for daily commuters as well as long-distance travelers. Being a major junction on the Central and Trans-Harbour lines, it connects seamlessly to key destinations like CSMT, Dadar, Kalyan, Panvel, Vashi, and Navi Mumbai. Local trains are very frequent, and coordination for Trans-Harbour routes is especially good.
The station is massive, with around 10 platforms handling an enormous volume of passengers every day. Despite the heavy crowd, train operations are quite efficient. Platforms are well connected through multiple foot overbridges, escalators, and lifts, making movement easier for senior citizens and differently-abled passengers. Digital display boards, good lighting, CCTV cameras, and clear announcements add to passenger convenience and safety.
Cleanliness is generally good considering the rush, and cleaning staff can be seen throughout the day. Toilets and waiting areas are available, though during peak hours everything feels extremely crowded. The platforms are mostly covered, which is very helpful during monsoons. There are ample food stalls, tea points, bookshops, and snack counters on the platforms, so passengers can easily grab refreshments while traveling.
One of the biggest advantages of Thane station is its excellent integration with other modes of transport. The direct and smooth connection to the bus stand is outstanding, and bus drivers and conductors are often seen guiding passengers. Auto-rickshaws, taxis, and app-based cabs like Ola and Uber are easily available outside the station. The surrounding area is full of markets, shops, fruit vendors, and restaurants, making it a very lively place.
The only real challenge is the crowd. During weekdays and peak hours, the station gets extremely congested, sometimes leaving very little walking space. Boarding trains can be tough, especially with luggage or during office hours. However, this crowd itself reflects how crucial and well-connected the station is.
Overall, Thane Railway Station does an impressive job managing a huge number of travelers every single day. With great connectivity, frequent trains, essential facilities, and strong links to buses and other transport, it remains one of the best and most important stations in the Mumbai region. Despite the rush, it delivers a reliable and efficient experience—definitely deserving of a 5-star rating

featured_reviews.name: Nitish Patel
featured_reviews.review_text:
Thane Railway Station, despite being one of the busiest and most important stations in Mumbai’s railway network, is extremely poorly managed. The entire system feels unplanned and outdated. Private vehicles and cabs are not allowed near the main entrance, making it very inconvenient for passengers — especially those with luggage, senior citizens, or families. You have to walk quite a distance just to find a cab or auto, which is unacceptable for a major junction.

The crowd management is chaotic, particularly during rush hours. Out of nearly 10 platforms, only 1 or 2 have escalators, and even those are often overcrowded or not working. Accessibility is a major issue that authorities seem to ignore completely.

The helper authorities at the platforms are mostly unresponsive — they usually sit idly and rarely offer help to passengers trying to find their platform or way out. The lack of guidance makes the overall experience frustrating.

And if the railway authorities cannot handle or provide a proper car parking facility, or build a structured parking system, then express trains shouldn’t even be halted at this station. It’s unfair to call Thane a major station when the basic passenger facilities are missing.

Overall, Thane station needs a serious overhaul — better planning, parking facilities, accessibility, crowd control, and staff accountability. For a key station in the financial capital of India, this level of mismanagement is truly disappointing.

featured_reviews.name: Amrish Sukhadiya
featured_reviews.review_text:
Words fall short for the magic I experienced at T Trikon’s Dehne campsite stargazing trip — it was nothing short of soul-stirring!

As soon as we stepped onto the plateau, the sight took my breath away: a row of vibrant orange, blue, green, and red tents glowing like jewels against the towering, flat-topped Sahyadri mountains bathed in molten gold from the setting sun. The sky was on fire — layers of orange, pink, and deep purple melting into each other while the sun slowly sank behind those ancient peaks, painting long shadows across the grassland. I just sat there, speechless, watching nature put on the most dramatic show I’ve ever seen.

Then night fell, and the real wonder began.

The stargazing was pure poetry. Our guide Shreekumar Sir, incredibly passionate and patient, set up this beautiful white telescope “Sanjaya” (named after Sanjay from Mahabharata) and took us on a cosmic journey. He didn’t just point out stars — he brought the sky to life with stories:

- The fierce Greek hunter Orion forever chasing the scorpion across the heavens
- Callisto transformed into the Great Bear (Ursa Major), circling the North Star
- Vain Queen Cassiopeia eternally sitting on her throne in the W-shape
- The inseparable twins Castor & Pollux, one mortal, one divine, bound together in the stars
- Mighty Heracles strangling the Nemean Lion (Leo), its heart marked by the regal star Regulus
- Zeus turning into a majestic white bull to carry away Europa (Taurus), with fiery-eyed Aldebaran glaring from the bull’s face

And then the beautiful Indian parallels — Rohini as the Moon’s beloved, Krittika nurturing Kartikeya, Ashwini Kumaras healing the gods, Sharmistha and Devyani’s tale of rivalry turning to renewal in Punarvasu… And one that moved me deeply: the story of **Saptarishi** and **Krittika**.

The guide pointed to the bright seven stars of the Big Dipper (Saptarishi — the eternal Seven Sages, wise guardians of Vedic knowledge, circling steadfast Dhruva like unchanging dharma). He explained how Agni (the fire god) became infatuated with the beautiful wives of these sages (the Krittikas). When they rejected him out of loyalty, Svaha (Agni’s devoted wife) tricked him by shapeshifting into six of them (except steadfast Arundhati, wife of Vashistha, whose purity made her impossible to imitate).
The six Krittikas ascended to the heavens as the sparkling Pleiades cluster (Krittika Nakshatra), shining eternally as symbols of nurturing fire, purification, and motherhood — while Arundhati remained faithfully beside Vashistha in the Saptarishi group, a beacon of unwavering devotion. Hearing this tale of desire, misunderstanding, sacrifice, and ultimate renewal while gazing at the twinkling Pleiades and the circling Big Dipper felt profoundly moving — like the stars themselves were whispering ancient lessons of balance, loyalty, and transformation right above us!

Around 12:30 am, when the cold started biting and eyelids grew heavy, they brought out steaming hot masala chai — the perfect midnight pick-me-up. Sipping that warm, fragrant tea under a blanket of stars, chatting with fellow stargazers, was one of the coziest, most magical moments of the night.
And the food? Oh my god, the food!
I had requested Jain food in advance and they happily prepared a delicious no-onion-no-garlic version that tasted just as soul-satisfying. Every bite felt like love from a Maharashtrian home kitchen.

The entire setup was spotless, the team warm and super helpful, the vibe relaxed yet full of wonder. Escaping Mumbai’s light pollution to this pristine corner of the Sahyadris, surrounded by mountains, myths, stars— it was everything I didn’t know I needed.

T Trikon didn’t just organize a trip; they created memories that will stay with me forever.
I’m already counting days till my next one — maybe winter for Orion or monsoon for the misty mountains!
Absolute 5 stars. Highly, highly recommended. You owe it to your soul.

– Amrish Sukhadiya
